- The king had sworn privately that a particular son would succeed him (1Kgs 1:13, 1Kgs 1:17, 1Kgs 1:30)
- The new king rides the old king's mule to his anointing (1Kgs 1:33, 1Kgs 1:38, 1Kgs 1:44)
- A king is anointed at a spring (1Kgs 1:33, 1Kgs 1:34, 1Kgs 1:38, 1Kgs 1:45)
- The people's shouting is so loud the earth splits (1Kgs 1:40)
- News of the rival's coronation reaches the pretender's feast and the guests scatter (1Kgs 1:42, 1Kgs 1:43, 1Kgs 1:49)
- The aged king bows in worship upon his bed (1Kgs 1:47, 1Kgs 1:48)

**David's charge to Solomon, death and burial**
- The dying king charges his successor to be strong and keep God's law (1Kgs 2:1, 1Kgs 2:2, 1Kgs 2:3, 1Kgs 2:4)
- Death called 'going the way of all the earth' (1Kgs 2:2)
- The dying king instructs his successor to execute old enemies (1Kgs 2:5, 1Kgs 2:6, 1Kgs 2:8, 1Kgs 2:9)
- The king 'slept with his fathers' and was buried in the City of David (1Kgs 2:10)

**Solomon executes Adonijah, Joab and Shimei and banishes Abiathar**
- The elder brother admits the kingdom passed to his brother by God's will (1Kgs 2:15)
- The king seats his mother on a throne at his right hand (1Kgs 2:19, 1Kgs 2:20)
- The new king executes rivals and enemies of his father (1Kgs 2:23, 1Kgs 2:24, 1Kgs 2:25, 1Kgs 2:34, 1Kgs 2:46)
- A priest of the losing faction is banished to his estate and removed from office (1Kgs 2:26, 1Kgs 2:27)
- A suspect is confined to the capital and told he dies the day he crosses a boundary (1Kgs 2:36, 1Kgs 2:37, 1Kgs 2:38, 1Kgs 2:42)
- Runaway slaves flee to a foreign king and are retrieved (1Kgs 2:39, 1Kgs 2:40)

**Solomon allies with Pharaoh; worship at the high places**
- The king builds his palace, God's house and the city wall (1Kgs 3:1)
- People sacrifice at high places because the temple is not yet built (1Kgs 3:2, 1Kgs 3:3)

**Solomon's dream at Gibeon; he asks for a listening heart**
- God appears to the king in a dream at night at a sanctuary after sacrifice (1Kgs 3:5, 1Kgs 3:15)
- The new king calls himself a little child who does not know how to go out or come in (1Kgs 3:7)
- God also grants the riches and honor that were not asked for (1Kgs 3:12, 1Kgs 3:13)
- The king holds a feast for his servants after a revelation (1Kgs 3:15)

**The two harlots and the living child**
- Two women each claim the same living child before a judge (1Kgs 3:16, 1Kgs 3:17, 1Kgs 3:18, 1Kgs 3:22, 1Kgs 3:23)
- A mother lies on her baby at night, killing it, and swaps it for another's (1Kgs 3:19, 1Kgs 3:20, 1Kgs 3:21)
- The judge orders the disputed child cut in two to test the claimants (1Kgs 3:24, 1Kgs 3:25)
- The true mother is revealed by giving up her claim to save the child (1Kgs 3:26, 1Kgs 3:27)

**Solomon's officials and twelve district governors**
- King appoints twelve district governors, each supplying the royal table for one month of the year (1Kgs 4:7)
- King's daughters are married to his district officials (1Kgs 4:11, 1Kgs 4:15)
- The people are as numerous as the sand by the sea, eating, drinking and rejoicing (1Kgs 4:20)

**Solomon's dominion, provisions and wisdom**
- King rules all kingdoms from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt, who bring him tribute (1Kgs 5:1, 1Kgs 5:4)
- The quantities of flour, cattle, sheep and game consumed daily at the royal table are listed (1Kgs 5:2-3)
- God gives the king wisdom and 'breadth of heart' like the sand on the seashore (1Kgs 5:9)
- King's wisdom surpasses that of the people of the East, of Egypt and of named sages (1Kgs 5:10-11)
- King speaks three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs (1Kgs 5:12)

**Treaty with Hiram of Tyre; cedars and forced labor**
- Foreign king (Hiram of Tyre) supplies cedar and cypress from Lebanon for the temple in exchange for food (1Kgs 5:20, 1Kgs 5:22-25)
- Logs are floated as rafts by sea to the building site (1Kgs 5:23)

**The temple's dating, dimensions and the divine promise**
- Temple building dated 480 years after the exodus, in the fourth year of the king, month Ziv (1Kgs 6:1)
- Three stories of side chambers around the temple, each wider by a cubit, resting on stepped ledges (1Kgs 6:5-6, 1Kgs 6:8, 1Kgs 6:10)
- Temple built of stones finished at the quarry, so no hammer, axe or iron tool was heard in the house (1Kgs 6:7)

**Cedar paneling, gold, the inner sanctuary and the cherubim**
- The inner sanctuary (devir) is a perfect cube of twenty cubits overlaid with pure gold (1Kgs 6:20-22)
- Two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high, whose outstretched wings span the inner sanctuary wall to wall (1Kgs 6:23-28)
- Temple walls and doors are carved with cherubim, palm trees and open flowers, overlaid with gold (1Kgs 6:18, 1Kgs 6:29, 1Kgs 6:32, 1Kgs 6:35)
- The temple takes seven years to build, completed in the eighth month (Bul) (1Kgs 6:37-38)

**Solomon's palace complex**
- King spends thirteen years on his own palace (contrast with seven for the temple) (1Kgs 7:1)
- Royal hall called 'House of the Forest of Lebanon', built on rows of cedar pillars (1Kgs 7:2-5)
- King builds a throne hall where he sits to give judgment (1Kgs 7:7)

**Hiram the bronze-smith and the pillars Jachin and Boaz**
- Master bronze-smith is son of an Israelite widow and a Tyrian father, filled with wisdom and skill (1Kgs 7:14)
- Pillar capitals with lily work, chain-network and rows of pomegranates (1Kgs 7:16-20, 1Kgs 7:22)

**The bronze sea, wheeled stands and temple vessels**
- Ten wheeled bronze stands decorated with lions, oxen, cherubim and palms carry basins (1Kgs 7:27-37)
- Ten golden lampstands stand before the inner sanctuary, five on each side (1Kgs 7:49)

**The ark brought into the temple; the cloud fills the house**
- Ark brought in procession into the temple at the autumn feast in the seventh month (1Kgs 8:1-2, 1Kgs 8:6)
- Ends of the ark's poles visible from the holy place but not outside, 'to this day' (1Kgs 8:8)

**Solomon's prayer of dedication**
- Exiles in an enemy land turn back with all their heart and pray toward their land, and God grants them mercy before captors (1Kgs 8:46-50)

**Final blessing, sacrifices and the dedication feast**
- Temple dedicated with a feast of seven plus seven days and a huge number of sacrifices (1Kgs 8:65-66)

**God's second appearance to Solomon**
- God appears a second time to the king, answering his prayer with promise and warning (1Kgs 9:2-3)

**Cabul, forced labor, building projects and the Ophir fleet**
- Gift of cities rejected as worthless and nicknamed 'Cabul' ('like nothing') (1Kgs 9:11-13)
- Pharaoh conquers a city and gives it to his daughter as a dowry on her marriage (1Kgs 9:16)

**The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon**
- Visitor confesses that reports did not tell even half of the king's wisdom and wealth (1Kgs 10:6-7)

**Solomon's gold, ivory throne, fleet and horse trade**
- Gold coming to the king each year weighs 666 talents (1Kgs 10:14)
- King makes hundreds of shields of beaten gold and hangs them in the palace (1Kgs 10:16-17)

**Solomon's foreign wives and apostasy**
- King has seven hundred royal wives and three hundred concubines (1Kgs 11:3)
- In his old age the wise king's foreign wives turn his heart to other gods (1Kgs 11:4)
- King builds high places for Chemosh, Molech/Milcom and Astarte on the mount facing Jerusalem (1Kgs 11:5, 1Kgs 11:7-8)

**Hadad the Edomite and Rezon of Damascus**
- God raises up a human 'satan' (adversary) against the king (1Kgs 11:14, 1Kgs 11:23, 1Kgs 11:25)
- A royal boy escapes a massacre to Egypt, marries into Pharaoh's family, and his son is raised among Pharaoh's sons (1Kgs 11:17-20)
- Exile at Pharaoh's court insists 'let me go' to return to his land after his enemy's death (1Kgs 11:21-22)

**Ahijah tears the cloak; Jeroboam flees; Solomon's death**
- Prophet tears a new garment into twelve pieces and gives ten to the future king as sign of the divided kingdom (1Kgs 11:29-31)
- The man designated to be king flees to Egypt (to Shishak) from the reigning king's attempt to kill him (1Kgs 11:40)

**Jeroboam's golden calves and rival cult**
- King invents a rival pilgrimage festival on the fifteenth of the eighth month, a month 'he devised from his own heart' (1Kgs 12:32-33)

**The man of God from Judah at Bethel**
- A prophet names a future king (Josiah) generations before his birth and what he will do (1Kgs 13:2)
- As a sign the altar splits apart and its ashes pour out (1Kgs 13:3, 1Kgs 13:5)
- The king's hand, stretched out against the man of God, withers and is restored at the prophet's prayer (1Kgs 13:4, 1Kgs 13:6)
- Prophet commanded not to eat bread or drink water in the place nor return by the way he came (1Kgs 13:8-10)

**The old prophet's lie and the lion**
- An old prophet lies, claiming an angel told him to bring the man of God home to eat (1Kgs 13:18)
- A lion kills a disobedient prophet but stands beside the body with the donkey, eating neither (1Kgs 13:24-28)
- Mourners lament 'Alas, my brother!' (hoy ahi) (1Kgs 13:30)
- Prophet asks to be buried beside the bones of the man of God (1Kgs 13:31)

**Jeroboam's wife disguised before blind Ahijah**
- Parent sends to a prophet to learn whether a sick child will recover (1Kgs 14:1-3)
- King's wife disguises herself to consult a blind prophet who recognizes her by her footsteps (1Kgs 14:2, 1Kgs 14:4-6)
- Gift of loaves, crumbled cakes and a jar of honey brought to a seer (1Kgs 14:3)
- The dynasty will be swept away as one burns up dung until it is gone (1Kgs 14:10)
- The sick child dies the moment his mother's foot crosses the threshold (1Kgs 14:12, 1Kgs 14:17)
- Israel struck like a reed shaken in water and scattered beyond the River (1Kgs 14:15)

**Rehoboam's reign and Shishak's invasion**
- The king's mother is named and is a foreigner (Naamah the Ammonite) (1Kgs 14:21, 1Kgs 14:31)

**Abijam and Asa of Judah**
- David did right all his life except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite (1Kgs 15:5)
- King sends the temple's silver and gold to a foreign king to break his treaty with a rival (1Kgs 15:18-20)
- The enemy's half-built fortress is dismantled and its stones and timber used to build one's own (1Kgs 15:22)

**Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha; Elah and Zimri**
- God raised the ruler 'from the dust' to be prince over his people (1Kgs 16:2)
- King is assassinated while drinking himself drunk in a steward's house (1Kgs 16:9-10)
- Usurper who reigned seven days burns the palace over himself and dies (1Kgs 16:15, 1Kgs 16:18)

**Omri founds Samaria; Ahab and Jezebel; Jericho rebuilt**
- The people split in half between two rival claimants to the throne (1Kgs 16:21-22)
- King buys a hill for two talents of silver and names the new capital after its former owner (Shemer, Samaria) (1Kgs 16:24)
- King marries Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and serves Baal (1Kgs 16:31)
- King builds a temple and altar of Baal in his capital and makes an Asherah (1Kgs 16:32-33)

**Elijah announces the drought and is fed by ravens**
- Prophet declares there will be neither dew nor rain except at his word (1Kgs 17:1)
- Prophet hides by a brook east of the Jordan and drinks from it until it dries up (1Kgs 17:3, 1Kgs 17:5, 1Kgs 17:7)
- Prophet hiding by a wadi is fed bread and meat morning and evening by ravens (1Kgs 17:4, 1Kgs 17:6)

**The widow of Zarephath and her son**
- God commands a foreign (Sidonian) widow to feed the prophet in famine (1Kgs 17:9-11)
- Widow gathering two sticks to bake a last meal for herself and her son before they die (1Kgs 17:10, 1Kgs 17:12)
- Prophet asks the starving widow to bake for him first, promising abundance (1Kgs 17:13)
- Bereaved mother accuses the man of God of coming to recall her sin and kill her son (1Kgs 17:17-18)
- Prophet carries a dead boy to the upper room, lays him on his own bed, and revives him (1Kgs 17:19, 1Kgs 17:21-22)
- Prophet stretches himself over the child three times, praying that his life return (1Kgs 17:21)
- A witness of the miracle confesses: now I know you are a man of God and God's word in your mouth is truth (1Kgs 17:24)

**Obadiah meets Elijah in the famine**
- Queen kills the prophets of YHWH (1Kgs 18:4, 1Kgs 18:13)
- Pious royal steward hides a hundred prophets, fifty to a cave, and feeds them bread and water (1Kgs 18:4, 1Kgs 18:13)
- King searched every nation and kingdom for the prophet, making them swear he was not there (1Kgs 18:10)

**Contest on Mount Carmel**
- Contest of gods: the god who answers by fire on an unlit sacrifice is God (1Kgs 18:23-25)
- Prophet mocks the silent god: perhaps he is musing, relieving himself, travelling, or asleep and must be woken (1Kgs 18:27)
- Prophets of Baal limp-dance around the altar and gash themselves with swords and lances till blood flows (1Kgs 18:26, 1Kgs 18:28-29)
- Prophet repairs the ruined altar with twelve stones for the tribes of Jacob (1Kgs 18:30-32)
- Sacrifice and altar drenched with four jars of water three times, filling a trench, before the miracle (1Kgs 18:33-35)
- The people fall on their faces crying 'YHWH, he is God! YHWH, he is God!' (1Kgs 18:39)
- The prophets of Baal are seized and slaughtered at the brook Kishon (1Kgs 18:40)

**Elijah prays for rain and runs before Ahab**
- Prophet on the mountaintop bows to the ground with his face between his knees praying for rain (1Kgs 18:42)
- Servant sent seven times to look toward the sea sees a cloud as small as a man's hand (1Kgs 18:43-44)
- Hand of YHWH upon him, the prophet girds his loins and runs ahead of the king's chariot (1Kgs 18:46)

**Elijah flees to Horeb; the still small voice**
- Queen swears by the gods to make the prophet's life like the slain prophets' by this time tomorrow (1Kgs 19:2)
- Despairing prophet sits and sleeps under a broom tree in the wilderness (1Kgs 19:4-5)
- An angel touches the sleeping prophet twice and gives him a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water (1Kgs 19:5-7)
- On the strength of one meal the prophet walks forty days and nights to the mountain of God (1Kgs 19:8)
- God twice asks the prophet 'What are you doing here?' and he twice answers the same complaint (1Kgs 19:9, 1Kgs 19:13)
- Prophet claims 'I have been very zealous for YHWH... and I alone am left' (1Kgs 19:10, 1Kgs 19:14)
- God passes by: a mountain-splitting wind, earthquake and fire, but God is not in them (1Kgs 19:11-12)
- After the fire comes 'a sound of thin silence' (qol demamah daqqah) (1Kgs 19:12)
- Whoever escapes the sword of the first avenger, the second will kill, and the third (1Kgs 19:17)
- God keeps a remnant of seven thousand whose knees did not bow and lips did not kiss Baal (1Kgs 19:18)
- Worshipers kiss the image of the god (1Kgs 19:18)

**The call of Elisha**
- The called man is plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, himself with the twelfth (1Kgs 19:19)
- Prophet calls his successor by throwing his mantle over him (1Kgs 19:19)
- Disciple called while plowing asks to kiss his parents goodbye first (1Kgs 19:20)
- Called disciple slaughters his oxen, boils the meat with the yoke for fuel, feeds the people, and follows (1Kgs 19:21)

**Ben-hadad besieges Samaria and is routed**
- A great king leads an alliance of thirty-two kings (1Kgs 20:1, 1Kgs 20:16)
- Besieging king demands the besieged king's silver, gold, wives and sons (1Kgs 20:3-7)
- Besieger swears the dust of the city will not suffice for handfuls for all his followers (1Kgs 20:10)
- Proverb: 'Let not the one who girds on his armor boast like one who takes it off' (1Kgs 20:11)
- Enemy king drinking drunk in booths with thirty-two allied kings is routed at noon (1Kgs 20:12, 1Kgs 20:16-21)
- Victory won by a small vanguard of 232 young men of the district governors (1Kgs 20:14-15, 1Kgs 20:17-20)

**Battle of Aphek; Ben-hadad spared**
- Enemies claim Israel's God is a god of the hills, not the valleys; God proves them wrong (1Kgs 20:23, 1Kgs 20:28)
- City wall falls on the 27,000 survivors who fled into it (1Kgs 20:30)
- Defeated men come to the victor wearing sackcloth on their loins and ropes on their heads to beg for life (1Kgs 20:31-32)
- Enemies rely on the reputation that the kings of Israel are merciful kings (malkhei hesed) (1Kgs 20:31)
- Victor calls the enemy king 'my brother'; envoys seize the word as an omen (1Kgs 20:32-33)
- Treaty grants trading quarters (hutsot) in the enemy capital and returns captured cities (1Kgs 20:34)

**The wounded prophet's parable against Ahab**
- Man who refuses a prophet's command to strike him is killed by a lion (1Kgs 20:35-36)
- Wounded prophet, disguised with a bandage over his eyes, tells the king a case and the king condemns himself (1Kgs 20:37-41)

**Naboth's vineyard**
- Commoner refuses to sell or trade his ancestral vineyard to the king: 'God forbid I give you my fathers' inheritance' (1Kgs 21:2-3, 1Kgs 21:6)
- Thwarted king lies on his bed, turns his face to the wall and refuses to eat (1Kgs 21:4-5)
- Queen writes letters in the king's name, sealed with his seal, ordering a judicial murder (1Kgs 21:8-11)
- A fast is proclaimed and two worthless men falsely testify that the victim 'blessed (cursed) God and king' (1Kgs 21:9-10, 1Kgs 21:12-13)
- Innocent victim is taken outside the city and stoned to death (1Kgs 21:13)

**Elijah's sentence on Ahab and Jezebel; Ahab's repentance**
- Prophet confronts the king: 'Have you murdered and also taken possession?' (1Kgs 21:19)
- King greets the prophet: 'Have you found me, O my enemy?' (1Kgs 21:20)
- King 'sold himself' to do evil, incited by his wife (1Kgs 21:20, 1Kgs 21:25)
- King tears his clothes, wears sackcloth, fasts and walks softly; God postpones the doom to his son's days (1Kgs 21:27-29)

**Micaiah son of Imlah and the lying spirit**
- God asks the heavenly council 'who will entice the king?'; a spirit volunteers (1Kgs 22:20-22)
- Prophet imprisoned on short rations of bread and water until the king returns in peace (1Kgs 22:26-27)

**Ahab's death at Ramoth-gilead**
- Dogs lick the dead king's blood at the pool of Samaria where harlots bathe (1Kgs 22:38)
- King builds a 'house of ivory' (1Kgs 22:39)

**Jehoshaphat of Judah and Ahaziah of Israel**
- Ships built to sail to Ophir for gold are wrecked at Ezion-geber (1Kgs 22:49-50)

**Ahaziah inquires of Baal-zebub; fire on the captains**
- King falls through the lattice of his upper chamber and is injured (2Kgs 1:2)
- Sick king sends to inquire of Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, whether he will recover (2Kgs 1:2-3, 2Kgs 1:6, 2Kgs 1:16)
- Rebuke: 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you go to inquire of a foreign god?' (2Kgs 1:3, 2Kgs 1:6, 2Kgs 1:16)
- Doom oracle: 'From the bed you have gone up on you shall not come down, but shall surely die' (2Kgs 1:4, 2Kgs 1:6, 2Kgs 1:16)
- Prophet identified by being 'a hairy man' (or wearing a hair garment) with a leather belt round his loins (2Kgs 1:8)
- Fire from heaven consumes two captains of fifty and their men sent to seize the prophet; the third begs and is spared (2Kgs 1:9-14)

**Elijah taken up in the whirlwind**
- Guild prophets at each town tell the disciple 'today God takes your master'; he answers 'I know, be silent' (2Kgs 2:3, 2Kgs 2:5)
- Prophet rolls up his mantle, strikes the Jordan, and the waters divide so they cross on dry ground (2Kgs 2:8)
- Disciple asks for a double portion (pi shnayim) of the master's spirit, granted if he sees him taken (2Kgs 2:9-10)
- Successor picks up the master's fallen mantle and repeats his miracle, striking the waters (2Kgs 2:13-14)
- Successor strikes the water crying 'Where is YHWH, the God of Elijah?' (2Kgs 2:14)
- Fifty men search three days for the ascended prophet, fearing the spirit dropped him on a mountain or valley, but do not find him (2Kgs 2:16-18)

**Elisha heals Jericho's water; the bears of Bethel**
- Prophet throws salt from a new bowl into the spring and heals the deadly, miscarriage-causing water 'to this day' (2Kgs 2:19-22)
- Small boys jeer 'Go up, baldhead!'; the prophet curses them and two she-bears maul forty-two of them (2Kgs 2:23-24)

**Jehoram's campaign against Mesha of Moab**
- A sheep-breeding vassal king pays tribute of a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams (2Kgs 3:4-5)
- Allied kings on a seven-day detour run out of water for army and beasts and despair (2Kgs 3:9-10)
- Prophet says he would not even look at the wicked king were it not for the righteous ally (2Kgs 3:13-14)
- Prophet calls for a musician; as he plays, the hand of YHWH comes upon him (2Kgs 3:15)
- Dry wadi fills with water though no wind or rain is seen (2Kgs 3:16-17, 2Kgs 3:20)
- Invaders fell every good tree, stop every spring and ruin every good field with stones (2Kgs 3:19, 2Kgs 3:25)
- At sunrise the water looks red as blood; the enemy thinks the kings have slain each other and rushes to plunder (2Kgs 3:22-23)
- Besieged king offers his firstborn heir as a burnt offering on the city wall, and 'great wrath' falls on Israel, who withdraw (2Kgs 3:26-27)

**The widow's oil**
- Creditor comes to take a dead man's two children as slaves for the debt (2Kgs 4:1)
- Widow's little oil fills all the borrowed vessels behind a shut door and stops when vessels run out (2Kgs 4:2-7)

**The Shunammite woman and her son**
- A wealthy woman has a small roof-chamber built for the holy man with bed, table, chair and lamp (2Kgs 4:8-11)
- Offered a favor with king or general, the hostess replies 'I dwell among my own people' (2Kgs 4:13)
- Woman protests the promise of a son: 'Do not lie to your maidservant' (2Kgs 4:16, 2Kgs 4:28)
- Child in the harvest field cries 'My head, my head!' and dies at noon on his mother's knees (2Kgs 4:18-20)
- Mother lays her dead son on the prophet's bed, shuts the door and rides to fetch him (2Kgs 4:21-24)
- Husband asks why she visits the prophet when it is neither new moon nor sabbath (2Kgs 4:23)
- Bereaved woman grasps the prophet's feet; the servant tries to push her away (2Kgs 4:27)
- Prophet admits 'YHWH has hidden it from me and not told me' (2Kgs 4:27)
- Servant sent in haste must greet no one and answer no greeting on the road (2Kgs 4:29)
- Servant lays the prophet's staff on the dead child's face but there is no voice or response (2Kgs 4:29, 2Kgs 4:31)
- Prophet lies on the child, mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, hands to hands, until the body warms (2Kgs 4:33-35)
- Revived child sneezes seven times and opens his eyes (2Kgs 4:35)

**Death in the pot; loaves for a hundred**
- Wild gourds in the stew make the prophets cry 'Death in the pot!'; flour thrown in makes it harmless (2Kgs 4:39-41)
- Twenty barley loaves of first fruits feed a hundred men with food left over, as God said (2Kgs 4:42-44)

**Naaman healed of leprosy; Gehazi's greed**
- A great foreign general, mighty warrior and favorite of his king, is a leper (2Kgs 5:1)
- A captive Israelite servant girl tells her foreign mistress that the prophet in Samaria could cure her master (2Kgs 5:2-4)
- Prophet sends word to wash seven times in the Jordan; the foreigner is cured (2Kgs 5:10, 2Kgs 5:14)
- Proud foreigner is angry that the prophet did not come out and wave his hand, preferring the rivers of his own land (2Kgs 5:11-13)
- Healed flesh is restored like the flesh of a little boy (2Kgs 5:14)
- Prophet refuses any gift for the healing (2Kgs 5:16)
- Convert takes two mule-loads of Israel's earth to worship YHWH on in a foreign land (2Kgs 5:17)
- Convert asks pardon in advance for bowing in the temple of Rimmon when his master leans on his arm (2Kgs 5:18-19)
- Prophet's servant runs after the healed man and lies to obtain silver and garments (2Kgs 5:20-24)
- Prophet reveals clairvoyance: 'Did not my heart go with you when the man turned from his chariot?' (2Kgs 5:26)
- The healed man's leprosy clings to the greedy servant and his descendants forever, white as snow (2Kgs 5:27)

**The floating axe-head**
- Prophet throws a stick into the river where a borrowed iron axe-head sank, and the iron floats (2Kgs 6:5-7)

**Elisha at Dothan; the blinded Arameans**
- The prophet tells the king even the words the enemy king speaks in his bedroom (2Kgs 6:8-12)
- At the prophet's prayer the servant's eyes are opened to see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire (2Kgs 6:15, 2Kgs 6:17)
- Enemy army struck with a blinding confusion (sanwerim) and led by the prophet into the enemy capital (2Kgs 6:18-20)
- Captured enemies are given a great feast and sent home instead of being killed (2Kgs 6:21-23)

**Famine in besieged Samaria; the cannibal mothers**
- In the siege a donkey's head sells for eighty shekels and a quarter-qab of dove's dung for five (2Kgs 6:25)
- Two mothers agree to eat their sons in turn; after the first is eaten the other hides hers (2Kgs 6:28-29)
- When the king tears his clothes, the people see sackcloth underneath on his body (2Kgs 6:30)
- King swears to behead the prophet, blaming him for the disaster (2Kgs 6:31)
- Prophet calls the king 'this son of a murderer' (2Kgs 6:32)
- 'This evil is from YHWH; why should I wait for YHWH any longer?' (2Kgs 6:33)

**The four lepers and the end of the siege**
- Prophet foretells that by this time tomorrow fine flour and barley will sell for a shekel at the city gate (2Kgs 7:1, 2Kgs 7:16, 2Kgs 7:18)
- Skeptic scoffs 'even if YHWH made windows in heaven'; told he will see it but not eat of it, and is trampled (2Kgs 7:2, 2Kgs 7:17, 2Kgs 7:19-20)
- Four lepers at the gate reason that they will die anyway and go over to the enemy camp (2Kgs 7:3-5)
- God makes the enemy hear the sound of chariots, horses and a great army, and they flee abandoning their camp (2Kgs 7:6-7)
- Finders of plunder say 'this is a day of good tidings (besorah); if we keep silent, punishment will find us' (2Kgs 7:9)
- King suspects the abandoned camp is an ambush by feigned retreat and sends scouts (2Kgs 7:12-14)
- Fleeing army leaves the road to the Jordan strewn with garments and vessels thrown away in haste (2Kgs 7:15)

**The Shunammite's land restored**
- Prophet warns the family to emigrate because God has called a famine of seven years (2Kgs 8:1)
- The woman arrives to petition the king at the very moment the servant is telling him her story (2Kgs 8:4-5)
- On returning from seven years abroad, the woman petitions the king and her house, field and its produce are restored (2Kgs 8:3, 2Kgs 8:6)

**Elisha and Hazael; Ben-hadad smothered**
- Sick foreign king sends a lavish gift by forty camels to ask the prophet if he will recover (2Kgs 8:7-9)
- Prophet says 'tell him he will surely recover', though God has shown he will surely die (2Kgs 8:10, 2Kgs 8:14)
- Prophet fixes his gaze until the man is ashamed, then weeps at the atrocities the future king will commit (2Kgs 8:11-12)
- Self-deprecation: 'What is your servant, a dog, that he should do this great thing?' (2Kgs 8:13)
- Usurper smothers the sick king with a wet cloth spread over his face and reigns in his place (2Kgs 8:15)

**Jehoram and Ahaziah of Judah**
- Judahite king marries a daughter of Ahab and walks in the ways of the house of Ahab (2Kgs 8:18, 2Kgs 8:26-27)
- Edom and Libnah revolt from Judah's rule 'to this day' (2Kgs 8:20-22)
- Wounded king returns to Jezreel to be healed, visited by his royal kinsman (2Kgs 8:28-29)

**Jehu anointed king**
- A young prophet anoints the army commander king in an inner room with a flask of oil, then opens the door and flees (2Kgs 9:1-6, 2Kgs 9:10)
- Officers spread their garments under the new king on the steps, blow the shofar and proclaim 'Jehu is king!' (2Kgs 9:13)

**Jehu kills Joram and Ahaziah**
- Watchman on the tower reports an approaching company; messengers sent out do not return (2Kgs 9:17-20)
- Watchman recognizes the rider by his driving: 'he drives like a madman' (2Kgs 9:20)
- 'What peace, while your mother Jezebel's harlotries and sorceries are so many?' (2Kgs 9:22)
- Usurper draws his bow and shoots the fleeing king between the shoulders, through the heart (2Kgs 9:24)
- Slain king's body is thrown on the plot of the man his father murdered, fulfilling the oracle (2Kgs 9:21, 2Kgs 9:25-26)

**The death of Jezebel**
- Queen taunts the usurper: 'Is it peace, Zimri, murderer of his master?' (2Kgs 9:31)
- Eunuchs throw the queen down from the window; her blood spatters the wall and horses trample her (2Kgs 9:32-33)
- When they go to bury her, only her skull, feet and palms of her hands are found (2Kgs 9:35)
- The corpse will be like dung on the field so no one can say 'this is Jezebel' (2Kgs 9:37)

**Ahab's seventy sons and the kinsmen of Ahaziah**
- Guardians behead the king's seventy sons and send the heads in baskets; they are piled in two heaps at the gate (2Kgs 10:6-8)
- Usurper tells the people 'you are righteous; I conspired, but who killed all these?' (2Kgs 10:9-10)
- Forty-two kinsmen of the Judahite king are seized alive and slaughtered at the pit of Beth-eked (2Kgs 10:12-14)
- Jehonadab son of Rechab gives his hand, is taken into the chariot, and goes to see the king's zeal for YHWH (2Kgs 10:15-16)
- 'Come with me and see my zeal for YHWH' (2Kgs 10:16)

**Jehu's ruse against the worshipers of Baal; his reign**
- King feigns devotion to Baal, gathers all Baal's worshipers in vestments into the temple, and has them all killed (2Kgs 10:18-25)
- The temple of Baal is torn down and made into a latrine 'to this day' (2Kgs 10:27)
- As reward, the king's sons to the fourth generation will sit on the throne (2Kgs 10:30)
- God begins to 'cut off' parts of Israel, as the foreign king seizes all of Transjordan (2Kgs 10:32-33)

**Athaliah's usurpation and the hidden prince Joash**
- Deposed ruler tears her/his garments crying 'Conspiracy, conspiracy!' or 'Treason!' (2Kgs 11:14)
- A condemned person is taken out so as not to be killed inside the sanctuary (2Kgs 11:15, 2Kgs 11:16)

**Joash repairs the temple; the collection chest; assassination**
- A chest with a hole bored in its lid set by the altar to collect donations (2Kgs 12:10)

**Jehoahaz and Jehoash; Elisha's death and the miraculous bones**
- In answer to prayer God gives Israel an unnamed 'savior' (moshia) (2Kgs 13:4, 2Kgs 13:5)
- An army is reduced by the enemy to a tiny remnant ('like dust at threshing') (2Kgs 13:7)
- Prophet has the king shoot an arrow out of the window as a symbolic act of victory (2Kgs 13:15, 2Kgs 13:17)
- Prophet lays his hands on the king's hands on the bow (2Kgs 13:16)
- King strikes the ground only three times, so his victories are limited to three (2Kgs 13:18, 2Kgs 13:19, 2Kgs 13:25)
- A corpse thrown into a prophet's grave touches his bones and comes back to life (2Kgs 13:20, 2Kgs 13:21)

**Amaziah's war with Jehoash and the fable of the thistle; Jeroboam II**
- New king executes his father's assassins but spares their sons, citing the law of Moses (2Kgs 14:5, 2Kgs 14:6)
- A conquered city or rock is given a new name 'to this day' (2Kgs 14:7)
- A section of the city wall is broken down by the victor (2Kgs 14:13)
- Conqueror carries off hostages (bene ta'aruvot) along with treasure (2Kgs 14:14)
- God saves Israel out of pity for its affliction though the king does evil (2Kgs 14:26, 2Kgs 14:27)

**Azariah the leper; the usurper kings of Israel; Tiglath-pileser**
- God strikes a king with skin disease; he lives in isolation while his son rules (2Kgs 15:5)
- Prophecy that a dynasty will last to the fourth generation is fulfilled (2Kgs 15:12)
- Rapid succession of kings, each murdered by the next usurper (2Kgs 15:10, 2Kgs 15:14, 2Kgs 15:25, 2Kgs 15:30)
- A usurper reigns only a month (or days) before being killed (2Kgs 15:13)
- Conqueror rips open the pregnant women of a city (2Kgs 15:16)

**Ahaz sacrifices his son, buys Assyrian help and copies the Damascus altar**
- Vassal declares 'I am your servant and your son' to an imperial king (2Kgs 16:7)
- King copies the design of a foreign altar and installs it in the temple (2Kgs 16:10, 2Kgs 16:11)
- The king personally approaches the altar and offers sacrifice (2Kgs 16:12, 2Kgs 16:13)
- The old bronze altar is reserved for the king 'to inquire' (divination) (2Kgs 16:14, 2Kgs 16:15)
- The temple's bronze stands and the sea on bronze oxen are dismantled (2Kgs 16:17, 2Kgs 16:18)

**Fall of Samaria and the sermon on Israel's exile**
- Vassal king withholds tribute and seeks help from Egypt, and is imprisoned (2Kgs 17:4)
- God warned the people by all his prophets and seers, 'Turn from your evil ways', but they would not listen (2Kgs 17:13, 2Kgs 17:14)

**The resettled peoples, the lions and the syncretistic cult of Samaria**
- Empire settles foreign peoples in the cities of a deported population (2Kgs 17:24)
- God sends lions to kill settlers who do not know the 'law of the god of the land' (2Kgs 17:25, 2Kgs 17:26)
- Each land has a god whose 'manner' (mishpat) newcomers must learn (2Kgs 17:26, 2Kgs 17:27)
- A deported priest is sent back to teach the settlers how to fear the local god (2Kgs 17:27, 2Kgs 17:28)
- Catalogue of foreign gods brought by settler peoples (Succoth-benoth, Nergal, Ashima, Nibhaz, Tartak, Adrammelech, Anammelech) (2Kgs 17:30, 2Kgs 17:31)

**Hezekiah's reform; Sennacherib's invasion and the Rabshakeh's speech**
- King smashes the bronze serpent made by Moses, called Nehushtan, because people burned incense to it (2Kgs 18:4)

**Manasseh's apostasy and its doom-oracle; Amon's assassination**
- The worst king rebuilds the high places, sets up altars to the host of heaven in the temple and practices every forbidden rite (2Kgs 21:2, 2Kgs 21:3, 2Kgs 21:11)
- King appoints mediums (ov) and wizards (yidde'oni) and practices soothsaying (2Kgs 21:6)
- God will wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish, wiping it and turning it upside down (2Kgs 21:13)
- Kings buried in the garden of their palace (garden of Uzza) (2Kgs 21:18, 2Kgs 21:26)

**Josiah's temple repair, the finding of the book and Huldah's oracle**
- A newly found sacred book is read aloud before the king, who tears his clothes (2Kgs 22:10, 2Kgs 22:11)

**Josiah's covenant, purge of the cults and Passover; death at Megiddo**
- Idolatrous cult objects are burned and their dust carried away or thrown on graves (2Kgs 23:4, 2Kgs 23:6, 2Kgs 23:12, 2Kgs 23:15)
- Women weave 'houses' (garments, hangings) for Asherah in the temple precinct (2Kgs 23:7)
- Priests of the high places may not serve at the altar but eat unleavened bread among their brothers (2Kgs 23:8, 2Kgs 23:9)
- The Tophet in the valley of Ben-hinnom is defiled so no one may burn children to Molech (2Kgs 23:10)
- Horses dedicated to the sun at the temple entrance and chariots of the sun burned (2Kgs 23:11)
- The high places Solomon built on the 'mount of destruction' (Mount of Olives) for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom (2Kgs 23:13)
- An old prophecy (naming the future king) is fulfilled generations later (2Kgs 23:16, 2Kgs 23:17)
- The bones of a prophet are left undisturbed when other graves are desecrated (2Kgs 23:17, 2Kgs 23:18)
- Priests of the high places are slaughtered on their own altars (2Kgs 23:20)
- A Passover such as had not been kept since the days of the judges (2Kgs 23:21, 2Kgs 23:22, 2Kgs 23:23)
- Despite the righteous king's reform, God does not turn from his anger over a predecessor's sins (2Kgs 23:26, 2Kgs 23:27)
- The righteous king is killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Necho (2Kgs 23:29, 2Kgs 23:30)

**Nebuchadnezzar's first conquest and the exile of Jehoiachin**
- God sends bands of raiders from surrounding nations against his people (2Kgs 24:2)
- King goes out to surrender to the besieger with his mother, servants and officials (2Kgs 24:12)

**The siege and destruction of Jerusalem; Gedaliah; Jehoiachin released**
- The temple, palace and great houses are burned by the conqueror's chief of guards (rav tabbahim) (2Kgs 25:8, 2Kgs 25:9)
- Only the poorest of the land are left behind as vinedressers and farmers (2Kgs 25:12)
- The bronze pillars, stands and sea are broken up and their bronze carried away (2Kgs 25:13, 2Kgs 25:14, 2Kgs 25:15, 2Kgs 25:16)
- Temple pillars eighteen cubits high with bronze capitals, network and pomegranates (2Kgs 25:17)
- Exiled king's head is 'lifted up' from prison; he changes his prison garments and eats at the conqueror's table (2Kgs 25:27, 2Kgs 25:29, 2Kgs 25:30)

**Genealogy from Adam to Abraham and the table of nations**
- History of the chosen people begins with a genealogy from the first man (1Chr 1:1)
- Genealogy given as a bare list of names with no verbs (Adam, Seth, Enosh...) (1Chr 1:1, 1Chr 1:2, 1Chr 1:3, 1Chr 1:24, 1Chr 1:25, 1Chr 1:26)
- Ten generations from the flood hero (or Shem) to Abraham (1Chr 1:24, 1Chr 1:25, 1Chr 1:26, 1Chr 1:27)
- Abram is Abraham: the patriarch's change of name noted (1Chr 1:27)

**Sons of Ishmael, Keturah and Esau; the Seirite chiefs and kings of Edom**
- Abraham's sons by the concubine Keturah (Midian, Sheba, Dedan...) (1Chr 1:32, 1Chr 1:33)

**Sons of Israel; the genealogy of Judah, Hezron, Jerahmeel and Caleb**
- A genealogy pauses to note an ancestor's sin or death at God's hand (1Chr 2:3, 1Chr 2:7)
- A genealogy notes descent through a daughter-in-law union (Tamar and Judah) (1Chr 2:4)
- Famous sages Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Darda listed as sons of Zerah of Judah (1Chr 2:6)
- Achan is called Achar, 'troubler of Israel', in a wordplay on his sin with the ban (1Chr 2:7)
- David is listed as the seventh son of Jesse (1Chr 2:15)
- David's sisters Zeruiah and Abigail are mothers of his generals (1Chr 2:16, 1Chr 2:17)
- A genealogy notes a foreign (Ishmaelite) father (1Chr 2:17)
- The genealogy of the sanctuary craftsman Bezalel is traced (1Chr 2:20)
- Patriarch marries at sixty and fathers a son (1Chr 2:21)
- A son is born to the wife after the father's death (1Chr 2:24)
- Genealogy notes an ancestor 'died without sons' (1Chr 2:30, 1Chr 2:32)
- Man with only daughters marries one to his Egyptian slave to continue his line (1Chr 2:34, 1Chr 2:35)
- Clans of scribes dwelling at Jabez, linked to the Kenites of the house of Rechab (1Chr 2:55)

**Sons of David and the kings of Judah to the post-exilic descendants**
- The same person bears different names in parallel sources (Daniel/Chileab, Bath-shua/Bathsheba, Shallum/Jehoahaz) (1Chr 3:1, 1Chr 3:5, 1Chr 3:15)
- A king's daughter (Tamar) is named at the end of the list of his sons (1Chr 3:9)
- The royal Davidic line is traced through the exile to post-exilic descendants (Zerubbabel and after) (1Chr 3:17, 1Chr 3:19, 1Chr 3:24)

**Clans of Judah; the prayer of Jabez; craft guilds; Bithiah daughter of Pharaoh**
- Man named for his mother's pain (otsev) prays to be blessed, have his border enlarged and be kept from pain, and God grants it (1Chr 4:9, 1Chr 4:10)
- A place called 'Valley of Craftsmen' because its founders were craftsmen (1Chr 4:14)
- Clans as hereditary guilds (linen-workers, potters) who dwelt with the king in his work (1Chr 4:21, 1Chr 4:23)
- Gloss: 'and the records/words are ancient' (1Chr 4:22)

**Simeon's genealogy, towns and migrations against Ham, the Meunim and Amalek**
- A tribe did not multiply like Judah; its families stayed few (1Chr 4:27)
- Clan leaders migrate seeking fat pasture for their flocks and dispossess the peaceful earlier inhabitants (1Chr 4:39, 1Chr 4:40, 1Chr 4:41)
- The last surviving remnant of Amalek is destroyed (1Chr 4:42, 1Chr 4:43)

**Reuben, Gad and half-Manasseh; the Hagrite war and the Assyrian exile**
- Reuben's birthright passes to Joseph while leadership (nagid) goes to Judah (1Chr 5:1, 1Chr 5:2)
- A person named Gog appears in an Israelite genealogy (1Chr 5:4)
- Genealogies registered (hityahes) at a dated time, in the days of named kings (1Chr 5:7, 1Chr 5:17)
- Transjordanian tribes war against the Hagrites (Arabian descendants of Hagar: Jetur, Naphish, Nodab) (1Chr 5:10, 1Chr 5:19)
- Warriors cry out to God in battle and he answers because they trusted him (1Chr 5:20)
- Huge spoil of camels, sheep, donkeys and captives listed in round numbers (1Chr 5:21)
- Many fell 'because the war was from God' (1Chr 5:22)

**Levite clans, David's singers and the Levitical cities**
- The prophet Samuel is placed in a Levite (Kohathite) genealogy (1Chr 6:13, 1Chr 6:18)
- Aaron's sons alone burn incense and make atonement for Israel (1Chr 6:34)

**Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim and Asher**
- Clan genealogies double as a military muster with counts of mighty men of valor (1Chr 7:2, 1Chr 7:5, 1Chr 7:7, 1Chr 7:9, 1Chr 7:11, 1Chr 7:40)
- A clan's warriors were numerous 'because they had many wives and sons' (1Chr 7:4)
- A tribe (Dan, Zebulun) is missing or barely present in the tribal genealogies (1Chr 7:12, 1Chr 7:13)
- A tribe descends partly through an Aramean concubine (1Chr 7:14)
- Genealogy notes that a man (Zelophehad) had only daughters (1Chr 7:15)
- An ancestress is called Hammolecheth, 'the one who reigns' (the queen) (1Chr 7:18)
- A patriarch's sons are killed by natives of Gath while trying to take their cattle (1Chr 7:21)
- The patriarch mourns many days and his brothers come to comfort him (1Chr 7:22)
- A son born after a family tragedy is named for the evil that befell the house (Beriah, 'in evil') (1Chr 7:23)
- A woman (Sheerah) builds towns (Lower and Upper Beth-horon, Uzzen-sheerah) (1Chr 7:24)
- Joshua son of Nun given a ten-generation genealogy from Ephraim (1Chr 7:25, 1Chr 7:26, 1Chr 7:27)

**The Benjaminites and the line of Saul**
- Man sends away his wives (divorces them) and fathers sons by another wife in Moab (1Chr 8:8, 1Chr 8:9)
- Benjamite warriors who were archers with 150 sons and grandsons (1Chr 8:40)

**The resettlers of Jerusalem; priests, Levites, gatekeepers and their duties**
- Judah was exiled to Babylon 'for their unfaithfulness' (ma'al) (1Chr 9:1)
- List of those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile by tribe and family (1Chr 9:2, 1Chr 9:3, 1Chr 9:9, 1Chr 9:13)
- Levite gatekeepers guard the temple on all four sides (east, west, north, south) in weekly shifts (1Chr 9:17, 1Chr 9:18, 1Chr 9:24, 1Chr 9:25)
- The gatekeeper offices were founded by David and Samuel the seer (1Chr 9:22)
- Levites lodge around the temple and are in charge of the key to open it each morning (1Chr 9:27)
- Sacred vessels are counted when brought in and taken out (1Chr 9:28)
- Only priests compound the ointment of spices (1Chr 9:29, 1Chr 9:30)
- The singers are exempt from other duties because they are at work day and night (1Chr 9:33)

**Saul's death on Gilboa and the theological verdict**
- The king, his three sons and his whole house die together on one day (1Chr 10:6)
- Victors send messengers to announce the good news to their idols and people (1Chr 10:9)
- The slain king's head (skull) is fastened in the temple of the enemy god and his armor dedicated there (1Chr 10:10)
- Loyal men retrieve the dead king's body and bury the bones under a tree, fasting seven days (1Chr 10:11, 1Chr 10:12)
- The king died for his unfaithfulness and for consulting a ghost-medium (ov) instead of God (1Chr 10:13, 1Chr 10:14)
- God himself turns the kingdom over to the new dynasty (1Chr 10:14)

**David anointed at Hebron and the capture of Jerusalem**
- The tribes acclaim the new king: 'We are your bone and your flesh' (1Chr 11:1)
- The elders make a covenant with the king and anoint him (1Chr 11:3)
- David captures the Jebusite stronghold of Zion, which becomes the City of David (1Chr 11:4, 1Chr 11:5, 1Chr 11:7)
- Whoever strikes the enemy first will be made chief; Joab goes up first (1Chr 11:6)

**David's mighty men and their exploits**
- Roster of the king's champions (the Three and the Thirty) with their feats (1Chr 11:10, 1Chr 11:11, 1Chr 11:26)
- A champion wields his spear against three hundred slain at one time (1Chr 11:11, 1Chr 11:20)
- Heroes hold a barley field alone when the people flee and win a great victory (1Chr 11:13, 1Chr 11:14)
- Foreigners (Uriah the Hittite, Zelek the Ammonite, Ithmah the Moabite) among the king's mighty men (1Chr 11:39, 1Chr 11:41, 1Chr 11:46)

**Warriors who joined David at Ziklag and the stronghold; Amasai's inspired greeting**
- Warriors who can sling stones and shoot arrows with right and left hand (1Chr 12:2)
- Warriors with faces like lions and swift as gazelles on the mountains (1Chr 12:9)
- Warriors cross the Jordan in the first month when it overflows all its banks (1Chr 12:16)
- The spirit 'clothes itself' with a man, who then speaks inspired words (1Chr 12:19)
- Inspired greeting 'Peace, peace to you and peace to your helpers, for your God helps you' (1Chr 12:19)
- A great army 'like the camp of God' (1Chr 12:23)

**Tribal contingents come to Hebron to make David king; the feast**
- Each tribe sends a numbered contingent to make the new king (1Chr 12:24, 1Chr 12:25, 1Chr 12:38)
- Issacharites 'who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do' (1Chr 12:33)
- Warriors come 'with a whole heart', 'not with a double heart', with one heart to make the king (1Chr 12:34, 1Chr 12:39)
- Three days of eating and drinking at the coronation, with provisions brought on donkeys, camels, mules and oxen (1Chr 12:40, 1Chr 12:41)

**Hiram's help, David's sons and the two victories over the Philistines**
- King inquires of God whether to attack and is told 'Go up, I will give them into your hand' (1Chr 14:10, 1Chr 14:14)
- God broke through the enemy 'like a bursting of waters' (1Chr 14:11)
- Enemies abandon their gods on the battlefield and the victor has them burned (1Chr 14:12)
- God puts the fear of the king on all the nations and his name goes out through the lands (1Chr 14:17)

**The Levites carry the ark to Jerusalem; musicians appointed; David dances**
- Only the Levites may carry the ark, on poles on their shoulders as Moses commanded (1Chr 15:2, 1Chr 15:15)
- The earlier disaster happened because they did not seek God according to the ordinance (1Chr 15:13)
- Levite musicians appointed by name to cymbals, harps on alamoth and lyres on the sheminith (1Chr 15:19, 1Chr 15:20, 1Chr 15:21)
- Obscure musical directions (al alamot, al ha-sheminit, le-natseah) also found in psalm headings (1Chr 15:20, 1Chr 15:21)
- Seven bulls and seven rams sacrificed when God helps the Levites carry the ark (1Chr 15:26)
- The king, wearing a linen robe and ephod, dances and leaps before the ark (1Chr 15:27, 1Chr 15:29)
- Michal watches from the window and despises the king dancing before the ark (1Chr 15:29)

**The ark installed in David's tent; Levite singers appointed**
- After offering sacrifices the king blesses the people in the name of YHWH (1Chr 16:2, 1Chr 16:43)
- At a festival the king gives every man and woman a loaf, a portion and a raisin cake (1Chr 16:3)
- Temple worship with cymbals, harps, lyres and priestly trumpets (1Chr 16:5, 1Chr 16:6, 1Chr 16:42)

**David's thanksgiving psalm (composite of Pss 105, 96, 106)**
- A psalm sung in the narrative is stitched from passages found in the Psalter (1Chr 16:8-22, 1Chr 16:23-33, 1Chr 16:34-36)
- The patriarchs few in number wander from nation to nation, protected by God (1Chr 16:19, 1Chr 16:20)
- 'Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm' (1Chr 16:21, 1Chr 16:22)
- Heavens, earth, sea, fields and trees rejoice and sing before the coming God (1Chr 16:31, 1Chr 16:32, 1Chr 16:33)
- The world is firmly established and cannot be moved (1Chr 16:30)
- Prayer: 'save us, gather us and deliver us from the nations' (1Chr 16:35)
- All the people say 'Amen' and praise YHWH (1Chr 16:36)

**Nathan's oracle of an eternal house and David's prayer**
- The king lives in a cedar house while the ark of God remains under curtains (1Chr 17:1)
- Pun on 'house': the king would build God a house; God will build the king a house (dynasty) (1Chr 17:10, 1Chr 17:12)
- Revelation described as God 'uncovering the ear' of his servant (1Chr 17:25)

**David's conquests and his officials**
- A king goes to 'set up his hand' (monument) at the Euphrates (1Chr 18:3)
- Bronze captured in war used for the temple's sea, pillars and vessels (1Chr 18:8)
- The Cherethite and Pelethite royal guard (1Chr 18:17)

**Envoys humiliated, the Ammonite-Aramean war, Rabbah taken, and the giant-killers**
- A king hires foreign chariots and horsemen with a thousand talents of silver (1Chr 19:6, 1Chr 19:7)
- At the turn of the year, when kings go out to battle (1Chr 20:1)
- The conqueror takes the gold crown of the enemy king or god and puts it on his own head (1Chr 20:2)
- Captives of a conquered city are cut with saws and iron picks (or set to labor with them) (1Chr 20:3)
- A giant's spear shaft is like a weaver's beam (1Chr 20:5)

**Satan incites the census; plague, the angel over Jerusalem and Ornan's threshing floor**
- Satan (or an adversary) stands up against Israel and incites the king to sin (1Chr 21:1)
- A king's census of the people is a sin that brings punishment (1Chr 21:2, 1Chr 21:3, 1Chr 21:7)
- The whole land 'from Beersheba to Dan' (1Chr 21:2)
- The commander protests the king's order but is overruled (1Chr 21:3, 1Chr 21:6)
- Let me fall into the hand of God, whose mercies are great, and not into the hand of man (1Chr 21:13)
- A destroying angel (mal'akh mashhit) is sent against the land or city (1Chr 21:12, 1Chr 21:15)
- The angel of YHWH is seen standing between earth and heaven (1Chr 21:16)
- King and elders clothed in sackcloth fall on their faces before the angel (1Chr 21:16)
- The landowner sees the angel while threshing and his sons hide (1Chr 21:20)
- At God's command the destroying angel returns his sword to its sheath (1Chr 21:27)

**David prepares materials and charges Solomon to build the temple**

- Levite males enrolled for temple portions from three years old (2Chr 31:16)

**Sennacherib's invasion, blasphemy and the angel's slaughter**
- Defenders stop up the springs and streams so the besieger will find no water (2Chr 32:3-4)
- King rebuilds the broken wall, raises towers and builds another wall outside (2Chr 32:5)
- Besieger mocks the king for removing high places and commanding worship at one altar (2Chr 32:12)
- The enemy king writes letters reviling the God of Israel (2Chr 32:17)
- Enemy envoys shout in Judean to the people on the wall to terrify them (2Chr 32:18)
- Enemies speak of Israel's God as of the gods of the nations, the work of human hands (2Chr 32:19)
- King and prophet pray together and cry to heaven against the invader (2Chr 32:20)
- An angel of God annihilates the besieging Assyrian army (2Chr 32:21)

**Hezekiah's illness and sign, pride, wealth, tunnel, Babylonian envoys and burial**
- King falls sick to the point of death, prays and receives a sign (2Chr 32:24)
- God gives the sick king a sign (wonder) that is not described (2Chr 32:24, 2Chr 32:31)
- King's heart grows proud after a favor, then he humbles himself and wrath is averted (2Chr 32:25-26)
- King builds treasuries for silver, gold, gems and spices, storehouses for grain, wine and oil, and stalls for cattle (2Chr 32:27-29)
- King blocks the upper outlet of the Gihon spring and channels it down to the west of the City of David (2Chr 32:30)
- God leaves the king alone to test him and know all that is in his heart (2Chr 32:31)
- A king's acts are said to be written in a prophet's vision or the words of seers (2Chr 32:32)
- Honored king buried on the ascent (upper part) of the royal tombs (2Chr 32:33)

**Manasseh's apostasy, captivity in Babylon, repentance and restoration**
- A king builds altars to and worships the host of heaven (2Chr 33:3, 2Chr 33:5)
- A wicked king builds altars to other gods inside the temple courts (2Chr 33:4-5)
- A king sets a carved image (semel) in the house of God (2Chr 33:7, 2Chr 33:15)
- A wicked king humbles himself in captivity and God hears his prayer (2Chr 33:12-13)
- A king taken captive to a foreign capital repents and is restored to his throne (2Chr 33:13)
- A repentant king's prayer is preserved in a prophetic record (2Chr 33:18-19)
- The Fish Gate of Jerusalem (2Chr 33:14)
- People still sacrifice at high places, but only to YHWH (2Chr 33:17)
- A king is buried in his own house rather than the royal tombs (2Chr 33:20)

**Josiah's early piety and purge of the land**
- While still a youth the king begins to seek the God of David (2Chr 34:3)
- Smashed idols ground to dust and strewn on the graves of their worshipers (2Chr 34:4)
- Bones of idolatrous priests burned on their own altars (2Chr 34:5)

**Temple repair, finding of the book of the Torah, Huldah's oracle and covenant**
- Money collected by the Levites is given to the workmen to repair the temple (2Chr 34:9-11)
- Levites skilled in music oversee the burden-bearers and workmen (2Chr 34:12-13)
- The scribe reads the found book aloud before the king (2Chr 34:18)
- Prophet announces that the curses written in the found book will come upon the land (2Chr 34:24)
- King stands at his place and makes the covenant before God (2Chr 34:31)

**Josiah's great Passover**
- King tells the Levites to set the ark in the temple: they need no longer carry it on their shoulders (2Chr 35:3)
- Levitical divisions follow the writing of David and the document of Solomon (2Chr 35:4)
- Levites prepare the Passover for priests, singers and gatekeepers who cannot leave their posts (2Chr 35:14-15)

**Josiah ignores Necho's divine warning and dies at Megiddo; Jeremiah's lament**
- A foreign king's warning is described as coming 'from the mouth of God' and ignored to the hearer's death (2Chr 35:21-22)
- Formula 'what have I to do with you?' (mah li va-lakh) (2Chr 35:21)
- Archers shoot the king, who says 'take me away, I am badly wounded' (2Chr 35:23)
- Mortally wounded king moved from his chariot to a second chariot and carried home (2Chr 35:24)
- A king dies in battle in the valley of Megiddo (2Chr 35:22)
- Male and female singers lament a fallen king every year as a fixed custom (2Chr 35:25)
- Jeremiah composes a lament for a dead king (2Chr 35:25)

**Last kings of Judah, burning of the temple, exile and seventy years**
- Overlord imposes a fine of 100 talents of silver and a talent of gold (2Chr 36:3)
- God's wrath rises until there is no remedy (2Chr 36:16)
- The enemy kills the young men by the sword in the sanctuary (2Chr 36:17)

**The edict of Cyrus closes the Hebrew canon**
- A canonical book ends with the summons 'let him go up' to Jerusalem (2Chr 36:23)

**Cyrus's decree and the return of the temple vessels**
- Event dated as fulfilling the word of God by the mouth of Jeremiah (Ezra 1:1)
- Neighbors equip the departing exiles with silver, gold, goods and cattle (Ezra 1:4, Ezra 1:6)
- An inventory's stated total does not match the sum of its items (Ezra 1:9-11)

**List of the returnees with Zerubbabel**
- Returnees' horses, mules, camels and donkeys are counted (Ezra 2:66-67)

**Altar rebuilt, Sukkot kept, foundation of the second temple laid amid weeping and shouting**
- Returnees rebuild the altar on its former foundations before the temple itself (Ezra 3:2-3)
- Burnt offerings resume from the first of the seventh month before the temple foundation is laid (Ezra 3:6)
- Cedars from Lebanon floated by sea to Joppa for the temple, paid with food and oil to Sidonians and Tyrians (Ezra 3:7)
- Temple building begins in the second month, as Solomon's did (Ezra 3:8)
- Temple foundation laid with vested priests blowing trumpets and Levites with cymbals (Ezra 3:10-11)
- Elders who saw the first temple weep aloud at the foundation of the second (Ezra 3:12)
- The sound of joyful shouting cannot be distinguished from the sound of weeping (Ezra 3:13)

**Offer of help from the deportee peoples rejected; opposition and accusations**
- Deported settlers claim they have sacrificed to Israel's God since the Assyrian king brought them (Ezra 4:2)
- Neighboring settlers offer to help build the temple and are refused (Ezra 4:3)
- The 'people of the land' weaken and frighten the builders and hire counselors against them (Ezra 4:4-5)
- Enemies write an accusation (sitnah) against the people to the king (Ezra 4:6)
- A letter written in Aramaic script and Aramaic language is quoted (Ezra 4:7)

**Rehum and Shimshai's letter to Artaxerxes and the king's stop order**
- Imperial officials list the deported peoples settled in Samaria (Ezra 4:9-10)
- 'The great and noble Osnappar' (Ashurbanipal) deported peoples to Samaria (Ezra 4:10)
- Imperial letters quoted with Aramaic chancery formulas ('and now', greetings of peace) (Ezra 4:11, Ezra 4:17)
- Officials denounce Jerusalem to the king as a rebellious and wicked city that will withhold tribute (Ezra 4:12-16)
- Officials justify loyalty because 'we eat the salt of the palace' (Ezra 4:14)
- Royal archives confirm that mighty kings in Jerusalem once ruled all Beyond the River (Ezra 4:20)
- Imperial decree stops the rebuilding until further order (Ezra 4:21-23)
- Narrative places documents of later reigns before earlier events (Ezra 4:8, Ezra 4:24)

**Haggai and Zechariah spur rebuilding; Tattenai's letter to Darius**
- Prophets (Haggai, Zechariah) urge and support the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 5:1-2)
- Provincial governor demands who authorized the building and the names of the builders (Ezra 5:3-4, Ezra 5:9-10)
- 'The eye of their God was upon the elders', so the work was not stopped (Ezra 5:5)
- Temple built of great (rolled) stones with timber laid in the walls (Ezra 5:8)
- Builders declare themselves servants of 'the God of heaven and earth' (Ezra 5:11)
- Exile explained to a foreign ruler: the fathers angered the God of heaven so he gave them to Nebuchadnezzar (Ezra 5:12)
- Sheshbazzar is credited with laying the temple foundation (Ezra 5:16)

**Cyrus's memorandum found at Ecbatana; Darius's decree; temple completed and dedicated**
- A lost royal memorandum is found in the archive of a distant citadel (Ezra 6:2)
- Building with three courses of great stones and one course of timber (Ezra 6:4)
- King orders daily supplies of animals, wheat, salt, wine and oil for the temple sacrifices (Ezra 6:9)
- Temple sacrifices include prayer for the life of the foreign king and his sons (Ezra 6:10)
- Violator of the decree is impaled on a beam torn from his own house and his house made a dunghill (Ezra 6:11)
- Edict closes with a curse on any king or people who alters it or harms the temple (Ezra 6:12)
- Completion credited to the decrees of Cyrus, Darius and Artaxerxes (Ezra 6:14)
- The second temple is finished on the third of Adar in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15)
- Twelve he-goats offered as sin offering by the number of Israel's tribes (Ezra 6:17)

**Passover of the returnees and those who separated from the nations' impurity**
- The Persian king is called 'the king of Assyria' (Ezra 6:22)

**Ezra's priestly lineage and journey to Jerusalem**
- A priest's genealogy traced back to Aaron the chief priest (Ezra 7:1-5)
- Hero called a skilled scribe (sofer mahir) in the Torah of Moses (Ezra 7:6, Ezra 7:11)
- The king grants the hero everything he asks (Ezra 7:6)
- The journey from Babylon to Jerusalem takes four months, first to fifth month (Ezra 7:8-9)
- The scribe set his heart to seek (study) the Torah, to do it and to teach it (Ezra 7:10)

**Artaxerxes' rescript to Ezra**
- Priest bears the imperial title 'scribe of the law of the God of heaven' (Ezra 7:12, Ezra 7:21)
- Royal grant up to 100 talents of silver, 100 kor of wheat, 100 baths of wine and oil, and salt without limit (Ezra 7:22)
- Emperor provides for the temple lest wrath come on his realm and sons (Ezra 7:23)
- Priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants are exempt from tribute, poll tax and toll (Ezra 7:24)
- Emperor empowers a priest-scribe to appoint judges who know the law of his God and teach those who do not (Ezra 7:25)
- Imperial decree enforces 'the law of your God and the law of the king' with death, banishment, fines or prison (Ezra 7:26)

**Ezra's doxology for the king's favor (start of first-person memoir)**
- Blessing God who put it into the foreign king's heart to glorify the temple (Ezra 7:27)

**Ezra's caravan, the search for Levites, fast at Ahava and the weighing of treasure**
- A descendant of David (Hattush) is listed among the returning exiles (Ezra 8:2)
- Leader reviews the caravan and finds no Levites, and must recruit them (Ezra 8:15)
- A center of Levites and temple servants in exile called 'Casiphia the place' (Ezra 8:17)
- Leader proclaims a fast at a river to seek a safe way for the journey (Ezra 8:21, Ezra 8:23)
- Leader is ashamed to ask the king for soldiers after boasting that God protects his seekers (Ezra 8:22)
- Gold, silver and vessels weighed out to priests for the journey and weighed again on arrival (Ezra 8:24-30, Ezra 8:33-34)
- Leader tells the bearers: you are holy to the LORD and the vessels are holy (Ezra 8:28)
- God delivers the caravan from enemies and ambushers on the road (Ezra 8:31)
- Twelve bulls offered for all Israel by the returned exiles (Ezra 8:35)
- Royal decrees delivered to the king's satraps and governors (Ezra 8:36)

**Report of intermarriage; Ezra's mourning and confession**
- The 'holy seed' has mixed itself with the peoples of the lands (Ezra 9:2)
- Leader tears his garment and robe and plucks out hair of his head and beard (Ezra 9:3, Ezra 9:5)
- Leader sits appalled until the evening offering, then rises to pray (Ezra 9:3-5)
- Our iniquities rise above our heads and our guilt reaches to heaven (Ezra 9:6)
- God gives the remnant 'a peg in his holy place' as a foothold (Ezra 9:8)
- God has punished us less than our iniquities deserved (Ezra 9:13)
- God has left an escaped remnant (Ezra 9:8, Ezra 9:13-15)

**Covenant to send away foreign wives; assembly in the rain; list of offenders**
- Leader prays and confesses weeping, prostrate before the house of God (Ezra 10:1)
- 'There is still hope for Israel concerning this' (Ezra 10:2)
- Community covenants to send away all foreign wives and their children (Ezra 10:3, Ezra 10:11, Ezra 10:44)
- Leader makes the priests, Levites and all Israel swear to carry out the reform (Ezra 10:5)
- Leader neither eats bread nor drinks water in mourning for the people's sin (Ezra 10:6)
- Whoever fails to attend loses his property (herem) and is separated from the congregation (Ezra 10:8)
- The assembly sits trembling in the open square in the winter rains (Ezra 10:9, Ezra 10:13)
- Named individuals are recorded as opposing the assembly's decision (Ezra 10:15)
- A tribunal of family heads examines each case at appointed times (Ezra 10:14, Ezra 10:16-17)
- Sons of the high priest are among those who married foreign wives (Ezra 10:18)
- Named list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:18-43)
- Mixed marriages have already produced children, who are included in the dismissal (Ezra 10:44)

**News from Jerusalem and Nehemiah's prayer at Susa**
- News that Jerusalem's wall is broken down and its gates burned (Neh 1:3)
- On hearing bad news the hero sits, weeps, mourns and fasts for days (Neh 1:4)
- A Jewish exile serves as cupbearer to the Persian king (Neh 1:11)

**The king's question, Nehemiah's commission and the night inspection of the walls**
- A courtier fears because his face is sad before the king (Neh 2:1-2)
- Jerusalem described to a foreign king as 'the city of my fathers' graves' (Neh 2:3, Neh 2:5)
- Courtier prays to the God of heaven before answering the king's question (Neh 2:4)
- The queen (shegal) sits beside the king as the courtier makes his request (Neh 2:6)
- King gives letters to governors to grant the traveler safe passage (Neh 2:7-9)
- Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite and Geshem the Arab oppose the rebuilding (Neh 2:10, Neh 2:19)
- Leader secretly inspects the ruined walls by night with a few men (Neh 2:12-16)
- A spring at Jerusalem called the Dragon (Tannin) or Jackal Spring (Neh 2:13)
- Builders are accused of rebelling against the imperial king (Neh 2:19)
- Leader tells the enemies they have no portion, right or memorial in Jerusalem (Neh 2:20)

**The builders of the wall and gates, section by section**
- High priest and priests build and consecrate a city gate (Neh 3:1)
- Nobles refuse to put their necks to the communal work (Neh 3:5)
- Goldsmiths, perfumers and merchants work as groups on the wall (Neh 3:8, Neh 3:31-32)
- A district ruler builds his section of the wall with his daughters (Neh 3:12)
- Each builder repairs the wall section opposite his own house (Neh 3:10, Neh 3:23, Neh 3:28-30)
- The pool of Shelah (Siloam) by the king's garden (Neh 3:15)
- The tombs of David used as a landmark on the wall (Neh 3:16)
- The 'court of the guard' beside the upper royal palace (Neh 3:25)
- The temple servants live on the Ophel (Neh 3:26)
- Province divided into districts and half-districts (pelekh) under named rulers (Neh 3:9, Neh 3:12, Neh 3:14-18)

**Sanballat and Tobiah mock the builders; Nehemiah's imprecation**
- Enemy ridicules the 'feeble Jews' reviving stones from heaps of burnt rubble (Neh 3:33-34)
- Mocker says even a fox climbing on the wall would break it down (Neh 3:35)
- The whole wall is joined up to half its height (Neh 3:38)

**Conspiracy against Jerusalem; builders work with a weapon in one hand**
- Neighboring peoples conspire together to attack the rebuilding city (Neh 4:1-2)
- A guard is posted day and night against attack (Neh 4:3, Neh 4:16)
- Workers' rhythmic complaint that the porters' strength fails and the rubble is too much (Neh 4:4)
- Neighbors warn 'ten times' of attack from every side (Neh 4:6)
- Defenders posted by families behind the wall with swords, spears and bows (Neh 4:7)
- God frustrates the enemies' plot once it becomes known (Neh 4:9)
- Half the men work while half stand guard with spears, shields, bows and armor (Neh 4:10, Neh 4:15)
- Builders work with one hand and hold a weapon in the other, swords at their sides (Neh 4:11-12)
- Trumpeter beside the leader: wherever the shofar sounds, rally there (Neh 4:12, Neh 4:14)
- 'Our God will fight for us' - rally at the trumpet call (Neh 4:14)
- Work continues from the rising of dawn until the stars come out (Neh 4:15)
- Leader and guards never take off their clothes while on watch (Neh 4:17)

**Outcry over debt slavery; Nehemiah's remission and his refusal of the governor's allowance**
- A great outcry of the poor and their wives against their fellow Jews (Neh 5:1)
- In famine the people pledge fields, vineyards and houses for grain (Neh 5:3)
- The poor borrow money against fields and vineyards to pay the king's tax (Neh 5:4)
- The poor protest: 'our flesh is like our brothers' flesh, our children like their children' (Neh 5:5)
- Parents forced to sell sons and daughters into slavery for debt (Neh 5:5)
- Leader shakes out the fold of his garment: so may God shake out whoever breaks the oath (Neh 5:13)
- Governor refuses his official food allowance so as not to burden the people (Neh 5:14-15, Neh 5:18)
- Governor feeds 150 officials and foreign visitors daily at his own expense (Neh 5:17-18)

**Plots against Nehemiah, the open letter, the hired prophet and the wall completed in 52 days**
- Enemies invite the leader to a meeting in the plain intending to harm him (Neh 6:2)
- 'I am doing a great work and cannot come down' - leader refuses a meeting (Neh 6:3)
- Enemy sends the same message four times, then a fifth with an open letter (Neh 6:4-5)
- Enemy sends an unsealed letter so its slanders can be read by all (Neh 6:5-7)
- Enemies allege the leader builds fortifications because he plans to make himself king (Neh 6:6-7)
- Enemies hire a prophet to frighten the leader into sin with a false oracle (Neh 6:10-13)
- A layman refuses to hide in the temple sanctuary to save his life (Neh 6:11)
- A prophetess and other prophets try to frighten the leader (Neh 6:14)
- The wall is completed in fifty-two days (Neh 6:15)
- Surrounding nations realize the work was done by God and are humbled (Neh 6:16)
- Local nobles exchange letters with the enemy, bound to him by oath and marriage (Neh 6:17-19)

**Gates guarded; underpopulated city; the genealogical register of the first returnees found**
- City gates not to be opened until the sun is hot (Neh 7:3)
- An official is appointed because he is a faithful man who fears God more than many (Neh 7:2)
- The city is wide and large but the people few and houses unbuilt (Neh 7:4)
- A list repeated elsewhere with differing figures (Neh 7:10, Neh 7:13, Neh 7:15, Neh 7:17)
- A parallel list lacks the horses and mules counted in its source (Neh 7:68)

**Ezra reads the Torah at the Water Gate; the day declared holy; Sukkot restored**
- Reader stands on a wooden tower made for the purpose, flanked by named men (Neh 8:4)
- When the reader opens the scroll all the people stand up (Neh 8:5)
- Assembly answers the blessing 'Amen, Amen' with uplifted hands and prostrates (Neh 8:6)
- Levites explain the Torah reading so the people understand it (Neh 8:7-8)
- Leaders forbid weeping and mourning because the day is holy (Neh 8:9-11)
- On the holy day the people eat, drink and send portions to those who have nothing (Neh 8:10, Neh 8:12)
- 'The joy of the LORD is your strength' (Neh 8:10)
- Studying the Torah, the leaders find a forgotten commandment written in it (Neh 8:13-14)
- Festival booths built on rooftops, in courtyards and in public squares (Neh 8:16)

**Fast of the twenty-fourth and the Levites' historical confession**
- The seed of Israel separate themselves from all foreigners (Neh 9:2)
- A quarter of the day spent reading the Torah and a quarter confessing and bowing (Neh 9:3)
- Levites stand on a platform and cry out to God with a loud voice (Neh 9:4)
- Call to bless God 'from everlasting to everlasting' (Neh 9:5)
- 'You give life to them all' - God sustains all creation (Neh 9:6)
- God chose Abram, brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and renamed him Abraham (Neh 9:7)
- God found Abraham's heart faithful (ne'eman) before him (Neh 9:8)
- God made known his holy Sabbath at Sinai (Neh 9:14)
- God gave his good spirit to instruct the people in the wilderness (Neh 9:20)
- God's ordinances are those 'which a man shall do and live by them' (Neh 9:29)

**The sealed pledge (amanah) and its stipulations**
- A written covenant document (amanah) sealed by leaders (Neh 10:1-2)
- Named list of those who sealed the covenant document (Neh 10:2-28)
- The people enter into a curse and an oath to walk in God's Torah (Neh 10:30)
- Pledge not to buy wares or grain from foreign traders on the Sabbath or holy day (Neh 10:32)
- Community pledges an annual third of a shekel for the temple service (Neh 10:33-34)
- Pledge: 'we will not forsake the house of our God' (Neh 10:40)

**One in ten chosen by lot to live in Jerusalem; residents of the city and the towns**
- One in ten of the people chosen by lot to live in Jerusalem (Neh 11:1)
- The people bless those who volunteer to live in Jerusalem (Neh 11:2)
- Jerusalem called 'the holy city' (ir ha-qodesh) (Neh 11:1, Neh 11:18)
- Judahite residents traced to Perez son of Judah (Neh 11:4-6)
- An Asaphite Levite leads the thanksgiving at prayer (Neh 11:17)
- A royal command fixes the singers' daily provision (Neh 11:23)
- An official stands 'at the king's hand' in every matter concerning the people (Neh 11:24)
- Resettlers live in towns with ancient names (Kiriath-arba, Beersheba, Ziklag) (Neh 11:25-30)
- A 'valley of craftsmen' (Ge-haharashim) (Neh 11:35)

**Lists of priests and Levites; the high-priestly succession**
- Levitical choirs stand opposite each other, watch facing watch, in antiphonal praise (Neh 12:9, Neh 12:24)
- A king called 'Darius the Persian' dates the priestly records (Neh 12:22)
- A 'book of the chronicles' is cited as a source (Neh 12:23)
- Gatekeepers guard the storehouses at the gates (Neh 12:25)

**Dedication of the wall with two thanksgiving choirs processing on the wall**
- Singers have built themselves villages around Jerusalem (Neh 12:28-29)
- Priests and Levites purify themselves, the people, the gates and the wall (Neh 12:30)
- Two thanksgiving choirs walk atop the wall in opposite directions and meet at the temple (Neh 12:31-40)
- Priests blow trumpets in a festive procession (Neh 12:35, Neh 12:41)
- Musical instruments attributed to David ('the instruments of David') (Neh 12:36)
- The rejoicing in Jerusalem is heard from far away (Neh 12:43)

**Ammonites and Moabites excluded; Tobiah expelled from the temple; Levites' portions, Sabbath and mixed marriages**
- A priest gives a foreign enemy a storeroom in the temple courts as his residence (Neh 13:4-5, Neh 13:7)
- Reformer throws an intruder's household goods out of the temple chamber (Neh 13:8)
- Temple chambers defiled by an outsider are purified and the holy vessels restored (Neh 13:9)
- The Persian king is called 'king of Babylon' (Neh 13:6)
- Unpaid Levites and singers abandon the temple for their fields (Neh 13:10)
- Treasurers appointed because they are counted trustworthy (Neh 13:13)
- City gates closed when they grow dark before the Sabbath and opened only after it (Neh 13:19)
- Merchants spend the night outside the wall waiting to trade, until threatened away (Neh 13:20-21)
- Purified Levites guard the city gates to keep the Sabbath holy (Neh 13:22)
- Children of mixed marriages speak their mother's language and cannot speak Judean (Neh 13:23-24)
- Reformer curses, strikes and pulls out the hair of the men who married foreign wives (Neh 13:25)
- Solomon, beloved of God, was made to sin by foreign wives (Neh 13:26)
- A grandson of the high priest is son-in-law of the Samarian governor and is driven away (Neh 13:28)
- The priesthood and the covenant of the priests and Levites are defiled by mixed marriage (Neh 13:29)

**Ahasuerus's banquets and Queen Vashti's refusal**
- King holds a banquet showing his riches for 180 days (Esth 1:3-4)
- At the royal banquet drinking is by rule, no one compelled (Esth 1:8)
- The queen holds a separate banquet for the women (Esth 1:9)
- Seven named eunuchs serve the king (Esth 1:10)
- Merry with wine, the king orders the queen brought in her crown to show her beauty to his guests (Esth 1:10-11)
- The queen refuses to come at the king's command and the king is enraged (Esth 1:12)
- A decree written into the laws of Persia and Media cannot be revoked (Esth 1:19)
- The disobedient queen is deposed and her royalty given to 'another better than she' (Esth 1:19)
- Royal decree that every man shall rule in his own house (Esth 1:20-22)

**The search for virgins, Esther made queen, and Mordecai foils the eunuchs' plot**
- Virgins gathered from all provinces so the king may choose a new queen (Esth 2:2-4)
- A royal eunuch keeps the harem and supplies the women's cosmetics (Esth 2:3, Esth 2:8, Esth 2:14-15)
- Hero's genealogy runs back to Kish the Benjaminite (Saul's father) (Esth 2:5)
- Hero's family was deported from Jerusalem with King Jeconiah (Esth 2:6)
- Orphan girl adopted and raised as a daughter by her cousin (Esth 2:7, Esth 2:15)
- Heroine has a Hebrew name (Hadassah) and a foreign one (Esther) (Esth 2:7)
- Heroine wins the favor of her guardian official, who gives her special treatment (Esth 2:9, Esth 2:15)
- Heroine at the foreign court hides her people and kindred on her guardian's orders (Esth 2:10, Esth 2:20)
- Twelve months of beautification: six with oil of myrrh and six with spices (Esth 2:12)
- Each maiden goes to the king for one night and passes to the concubines' house (Esth 2:13-14)
- Heroine asks for nothing beyond what the eunuch advises when she goes to the king (Esth 2:15)
- An orphan girl is loved above all and crowned queen (Esth 2:17)
- King grants the provinces a remission and gives gifts at the new queen's feast (Esth 2:18)
- Hero sits in the king's gate as an official (Esth 2:19, Esth 2:21)
- Two eunuch doorkeepers plot to kill the king; the hero learns of it and reports it (Esth 2:21-22)
- Convicted plotters against the king are hanged (impaled) on a tree (Esth 2:23)
- A courtier's service is recorded in the royal book of chronicles before the king (Esth 2:23)

**Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman; the lot is cast and the decree of extermination issued**
- Villain called 'the Agagite' opposes a hero descended from Kish the Benjaminite (Esth 3:1, Esth 3:10)
- King promotes a courtier and sets his seat above all the princes (Esth 3:1)
- Hero refuses to bow or prostrate himself before a powerful official (Esth 3:2-5)
- Courtiers press the hero day after day to obey the order, and he refuses (Esth 3:4)
- Offended by one man, the villain seeks to destroy his whole people (Esth 3:6)
- Villain offers the king ten thousand talents of silver for permission to destroy a people (Esth 3:9)
- King takes off his signet ring and gives it to a courtier to seal decrees (Esth 3:10, Esth 3:12)
- Decree to destroy, kill and annihilate an entire people, young and old, women and children, on a single day (Esth 3:13)
- King and his vizier sit down to drink while the city is thrown into confusion by their decree (Esth 3:15)

**Mordecai's mourning and Esther's resolve to approach the king**
- No one may enter the king's gate dressed in sackcloth (Esth 4:2)
- A mourner refuses the fresh clothes sent to replace his sackcloth (Esth 4:4)
- Anyone who enters the king's inner court unsummoned is put to death (Esth 4:11)
- Relief and deliverance will arise 'from another place' if the hero stays silent (veiled reference to God) (Esth 4:14)
- 'Who knows whether you came to royal power for such a time as this?' (Esth 4:14)
- Heroine resolves to risk death for her people: 'if I perish, I perish' (Esth 4:16)
- Deliverance narrated without any explicit mention of God (Esth 4:14)

**Esther before the king; first banquet; Haman's gallows**
- The heroine delays her real request, inviting king and villain to successive banquets (Esth 5:4, Esth 5:8)
- The villain boasts to wife and friends of his wealth, sons and honors just before his fall (Esth 5:11, Esth 5:12)
- The villain's wife and friends advise him to build a gallows for his rival (Esth 5:14)
- A stake or gallows fifty cubits high is erected for hanging the rival (Esth 5:14)

**The king's sleepless night and Mordecai's parade**
- A sleepless king has the royal chronicles read to him and discovers an unrewarded benefactor (Esth 6:1, Esth 6:2)
- The man who exposed a plot against the king's life has gone unrewarded (Esth 6:2, Esth 6:3)
- Asked how to honor 'the man the king delights to honor', the villain, thinking it is himself, prescribes the honor his rival receives (Esth 6:6, Esth 6:7, Esth 6:8, Esth 6:9)
- Honoree is dressed in the king's robe and paraded through the city on the king's horse with a herald (Esth 6:8, Esth 6:9, Esth 6:11)
- The villain himself must lead his rival's horse and proclaim his honor (Esth 6:10, Esth 6:11)
- The villain's wise men and wife foretell that he cannot prevail against one 'of the seed of the Jews' (Esth 6:13)

**Second banquet; Haman exposed and hanged**
- Queen protests that her people have been sold to destruction; had it been slavery she would have kept silent (Esth 7:3, Esth 7:4)
- The queen reveals her hidden ethnic identity to the king to save her people (Esth 7:3, Esth 7:4, Esth 7:6)
- The enraged king leaves the banquet for the palace garden and returns to a compromising scene (Esth 7:7, Esth 7:8)
- Villain falls on the queen's couch pleading, and the king takes it as assault (Esth 7:8)
- The condemned man's face is covered at the king's word (Esth 7:8)
- A eunuch informs the king that the villain's gallows stands ready (Esth 7:9)

**Mordecai elevated; the counter-decree**
- The condemned enemy's household is given to the intended victim (Esth 8:1, Esth 8:7)
- The king takes back his signet ring from the fallen vizier and gives it to the hero (Esth 8:2)
- A decree written in the king's name and sealed with his ring cannot be revoked (Esth 8:8)
- Since the first decree cannot be revoked, a second edict permits the threatened people to defend themselves (Esth 8:5, Esth 8:11, Esth 8:13)
- Mounted royal couriers on swift royal steeds carry the edict in haste (Esth 8:10, Esth 8:14)
- The hero goes out in royal blue and white with a great gold crown and a purple linen mantle (Esth 8:15)
- 'The Jews had light and gladness, joy and honor' (Esth 8:16)
- Many of the peoples of the land become Jews (mityahadim) because fear of the Jews fell on them (Esth 8:17)
